issue_summary: Open-source AID is not something you download and forget. The person (or a parent) has to build the app, keep it signed, update it, and keep a working set of phone, pump, CGM and sometimes a radio bridge. Loop, Trio and iAPS run only on iPhone. They are built either in a web browser (GitHub Actions to TestFlight, available since Loop 3.0 in January 2023) or on a Mac with Xcode. A browser build needs a paid Apple Developer account (US$99 a year). Each TestFlight build expires after 90 days, Apple distribution certificates expire yearly, and GitHub now switches off scheduled builds after 60 days of inactivity. A free-account Mac build has to be rebuilt every week. AndroidAPS builds also expire: an out-of-date build is pushed into low-glucose-suspend (or open-loop) mode. On top of the build come the hardware dependencies. Medtronic pumps must be older models with specific firmware. Omnipod Eros and Medtronic need a RileyLink-type bridge. Eros pods stopped shipping in the US in December 2023. Dexcom G7, 15-day G7, Libre and Omnipod 5 each needed new app releases before they worked. iOS and Android major updates have repeatedly broken or degraded looping. Recent problems include an iOS 26 interface bug, iPhone 16/17e Bluetooth problems with DASH pods, a sharp rise in DASH Atlas pod faults (Nov 2025 to Apr 2026), and G7 readings not reaching Loop or Trio (2025). The phone is a single point of failure: lose it, drain it or let the app expire, and automation stops. Loop then falls back to scheduled basal within about 30 minutes. Very little of this work happens in the clinic, and clinicians are generally not expected to troubleshoot it. Its effects still show up at visits as supply requests, gaps in data, unexplained open-loop periods and device switches.
who_is_affected: Adults who self-build, and above all parents and caregivers, who often maintain several apps at once (Loop or Trio plus LoopFollow and LoopCaregiver), each with its own expiry. Android-only, older-Mac and less tech-confident people are the most likely to be excluded. On the clinician side it reaches endocrinologists and diabetes educators, who prescribe pumps, pods and CGM, train on pumps (Omnipod training is a prerequisite), field questions after failures and write school or hospital letters. Hospital and ED staff meet a phone-dependent, unregulated system. Primary care is rarely involved.
system_specificity: Applies to all systems, in different forms. Loop, Trio and iAPS: iOS only, an Apple Developer account, TestFlight 90-day or annual certificate expiry, iOS-update risk, and iPhone 16/17e-with-DASH caveats. AndroidAPS: Android only (latest version needs Android 12+), APK expiry that enforces LGS, Android 15/16 Bluetooth regressions, and a browser build now recommended over Android Studio. OpenAPS: legacy rig hardware (Raspberry Pi or Intel Edison) and old Medtronic or Eros pumps [uncertain: not re-verified for 2026]. Loop and OpenAPS lean most on scarce legacy Medtronic pumps and RileyLink. DASH, Omnipod 5, Medtrum and Dana need no bridge.
care_setting: Mostly outside the clinic: at home and through peer communities. Inside the care system it surfaces at routine endocrinology and educator visits (pump, pod and CGM prescriptions, Omnipod training, device changes), in pediatric clinics (caregiver apps, multi-app upkeep, letters for school phone-ban exemptions [uncertain: DIY-specific evidence not found]), and in inpatient or ED care (phone and app must stay with the patient; BC Diabetes issues a hospital letter). Primary care is rarely involved.
trigger_moment: App or certificate expiry (90-day TestFlight, yearly certificate, weekly for a free-account Mac build, AAPS expiry date). A major iOS or Android update, or a new phone. A new CGM or pump generation, or a pump being withdrawn (G7, 15-day G7, Libre, Eros withdrawal, DASH Atlas faults, Omnipod 5). Changes to Apple or GitHub accounts and policies (unaccepted agreements, disabled workflows, token expiry). Supply or prescription refills. Hospital admission, travel, a lost or broken phone, or a pump fault.

key_sources.source: LoopDocs - Loop 3 release history (LoopKit, community documentation)
key_sources.relevance: Dated record of build-method changes (browser build in 3.0, automatic certificate renewal in 3.6.0), iOS-driven fixes (iOS 26 hotfix 3.8.1, 3.8.2), Xcode-driven forced updates (3.2.3 for Xcode 15; 3.4.2-3.4.4 expiry bug), hardware additions (G7 in 3.0, Libre in 3.4, 15-day G7 in 3.10, Eversense and Medtrum in 3.14.2, Omnipod 5 in 3.14.7) and fixes for G7 gaps and Omnipod connections. Ten releases between Jan and Nov 2026.

key_sources.source: LoopDocs - Browser Build update guide and intro summary
key_sources.relevance: Rebuild at least every 90 days; certificates renewed yearly; GitHub token defaults to 30-day expiry; Apple agreements, Digital Services Act non-trader setup, the two-certificate limit and disabled workflows are the common failure points. First-time setup 2-4 hours across several days, allow up to a week (https://loopkit.github.io/loopdocs/browser/intro-summary/).

key_sources.source: LoopDocs - Compatible computer, phone, pump and CGM pages
key_sources.relevance: Mac build needs 50 GB free and macOS 26.6+, and macOS 27 (Apple Silicon only) by spring 2027. Free account means a weekly rebuild. iPhone X and 8 unsupported; iOS 17.6 minimum; iPhone 16/17e-with-DASH caveat; 'you cannot go backwards' after an iOS update. Medtronic firmware limits (523/723 at 2.4 or lower; Veo at 2.6A/2.7A or lower). Eros US supply ended Dec 2023. Insulet does not support Loop. Libre 3 and Guardian unsupported. Related pages: https://loopkit.github.io/loopdocs/build/phone/ , https://loopkit.github.io/loopdocs/build/cgm , https://loopkit.github.io/loopdocs/build/computer

key_sources.source: Loop and Learn newsletters (community)
key_sources.sample_size: Community usage analytics; denominator not stated
key_sources.relevance: DASH Atlas pod faults: per-user monthly fault rate about 4% (Nov 2025) to about 18.5% (Apr 2026), across iOS 18.x-26.x and Loop 3.6-3.13; not seen on AAPS. Feb 2025: many reports of G7 readings not reaching Loop or Trio (https://loopandlearn.github.io/news/edition/2025-02-24). Apr 2025: Loop 3.6 G7 outage mitigation and GitHub sync breakage (https://loopandlearn.github.io/news/edition/2025-04-27).

key_sources.source: Loop and Learn - Version updates page (iOS/Xcode guidance)
key_sources.relevance: Treat the phone as a medical device. Turn off automatic iOS updates (iOS 27.2 turns them back on). Make sure you can build before upgrading iOS. Trio 1.0.x needs iOS 17.6+; LoopFollow 7 needs iOS 18.

key_sources.source: AndroidAPS documentation - Release notes and build methods
key_sources.relevance: Expiry warnings from 28 days out. 'After expiration LGS mode is enforced' (the intro says open loop instead; the docs conflict). Android 12+ required. Android 15 and 16 Bluetooth and Omnipod fixes. Browser build is now the recommended method (https://androidaps.readthedocs.io/en/latest/SettingUpAaps/BuildingAaps.html).

key_sources.source: Lum JW et al. A real-world prospective study of the safety and effectiveness of the Loop open source automated insulin delivery system. Diabetes Technol Ther 2021
key_sources.relevance: Recruited when ordering a RileyLink. Connectivity and communication problems were 27% of reported issues; hardware damage or failure 10%. 17% of time could not be classified (possible open-loop reversion). No formal customer support. 0 DKA; 1 severe hypo attributed to Loop.

key_sources.source: Wong JJ et al. Discontinued Use of the Loop Insulin Dosing System: A Mixed-Methods Investigation. Diabetes Technol Ther 2022;24(4):241-248
key_sources.relevance: Among discontinuers: 'not working properly' 22.2%, 'spent too much time on it' 22.2%, 'too complicated / could not find resources' 13.3%, hard to get supplies 4.4%, version not up to date 2.2%. One parent stopped for fear of provider disapproval.

key_sources.source: Suttiratana SC et al. Qualitative Study of User Experiences with Loop. Diabetes Technol Ther 2022;24(6):416-423
key_sources.relevance: Technical issues were the most-discussed drawback: RileyLink range, signal loss, trouble getting older pumps. The Facebook group served as an informal help desk. Many providers could not troubleshoot. Sample 95% white, 94% privately insured, 73% income of $100K or more.

key_sources.source: Huhndt A et al. Barriers to Uptake of Open-Source Automated Insulin Delivery Systems (caregivers, OPEN survey). Front Clin Diabetes Healthc 2022;3:876511
key_sources.relevance: 50% lacked skills to build. 42.9% feared they could not maintain the system. 35.7% found resources overwhelming. 33.3% did not know where to source parts (RileyLink or rig 77.8%, loopable pump 66.7%). 44.4% had no HCP support because of the team's limited technical expertise. 88.9% would be motivated if an HCP recommended it.

key_sources.source: O'Donnell S et al. Barriers to uptake of open-source AID systems: socioeconomic factors and perceived challenges of adults with T1D from the OPEN survey. Diabetes Res Clin Pract 2023;197:110235
key_sources.relevance: Main barriers: sourcing components, low confidence in technical skills, time and effort to build, and fear of losing HCP support.

key_sources.source: Cleal B et al. (Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen), open-ended survey of open-source AID users. J Med Internet Res 2025;27:e48406 (correction e72519)
key_sources.relevance: Getting the components and doing the technical setup were sometimes problematic. The #WeAreNotWaiting community was the main source of knowledge and support. A correction was published.

key_sources.source: Braune K et al. Open-source automated insulin delivery: international consensus statement and practical guidance for health-care professionals. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2022;10(1):58-74
key_sources.relevance: Users update manually and there is no call-in helpline. Building and using take different skill sets. Recommends in-warranty devices and warns about second-hand devices. Connectivity is among the most-reported concerns. HCPs should document discussions and note that the clinic cannot take responsibility for the system.

key_sources.source: Crabtree TSJ et al. ABCD DTN-UK and ACDC survey of UK HCP attitudes to OS-AID. Diabetes Ther 2022;13(2):341-353
key_sources.relevance: 73.5% were at most 'somewhat confident' describing OS-AID setup; 8.8% extremely confident. 91% uncomfortable starting the discussion (67% because it is unapproved, 63% own lack of knowledge, 28% did not want to invalidate an NHS pump warranty). 59% uncomfortable giving ongoing support; 94% would still provide care. Primary DOI: 10.1007/s13300-022-01203-5

key_sources.source: Morrison et al. Canadian Healthcare Providers' Attitudes Towards Automated Insulin Delivery Systems (medRxiv preprint)
key_sources.relevance: About 60% would support a patient's decision to use DIY AID. Median of 1-5 DIY users per practice (vs 6-24 for commercial), so clinicians see too few cases to build technical familiarity.

key_sources.source: Burnside MJ et al. Open-Source Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes (CREATE). N Engl J Med 2022
key_sources.relevance: Even with the trial supplying the phone and pump (modified AndroidAPS 2.8, DANA-i, G6), 2 AID participants withdrew for connectivity or hardware issues. No severe hypoglycemia or DKA.

key_sources.source: Diabetes Canada. Do-It-Yourself Automated Insulin Delivery: A Health-care Practitioner User's Guide. Can J Diabetes 2023;47(5):389-397
key_sources.relevance: Uses the term 'DIY' on purpose to stress that users build and maintain their own systems. Warns that its content may date quickly because developers iterate so fast.

key_sources.source: BC Diabetes - 'Looping at BCDiabetes' (SOS-AID) and 'Looping in hospital' letter (Dr Tom Elliott)
key_sources.sample_size: 3,694 clients installed (Loop, iAPS, Trio, AAPS); 347 children with LoopCaregiver
key_sources.relevance: Clinic builds the apps and hands out Loop through its own TestFlight and AAPS from its own cloud, free of charge. Requires an iPhone 13 or newer, or Android 9+. Asks users to turn off auto iOS updates because Dexcom 'typically lags about three months behind'. Requires a safety kit; peer Facebook group plus weekday email support. The hospital letter says the system is 'installed, configured & maintained by BCDiabetes staff' (https://www.bcdiabetes.ca/wp-content/uploads/bcdpdfs/Looping-in-hospital---letter-to-hospital-staff.pdf).

key_sources.source: FDA / Medtronic MiniMed 508 and Paradigm cybersecurity recall
key_sources.relevance: The recalled models and firmware are essentially the loopable Medtronic pumps. They cannot be patched and the replacement programme swaps them for non-loopable pumps, which shrank legitimate supply and pushed users toward second-hand pumps.

key_sources.source: Nightscout Foundation - Omnipod 5 open-source support FAQ
key_sources.relevance: Loop 3.14.7 and Trio 1.0.0 (15 Sep 2026) support Omnipod 5 pods; AAPS is in open beta. No bridge is needed, and there is no sign of the iPhone 16/17e problems seen with DASH Atlas pods. Not endorsed by Insulet.

key_sources.source: Tidepool Loop FDA clearance (K203689) and Sequel twiist
key_sources.year: Jan 2023 (Tidepool Loop); twiist app on App Store Apr 2025; full US launch early 2026
key_sources.relevance: Cleared derivatives of the Loop algorithm come through the App Store with manufacturer support and no self-build, expiry or certificate work. Tidepool Loop reaches patients through partner products such as twiist (https://diatribe.org/diabetes-technology/fda-clears-twiist-automated-insulin-delivery-system).

key_sources.source: Reddit r/AndroidAPS thread: 'AndroidAPS stuck on open loop after 2 years'
key_sources.relevance: A user's AAPS dropped out of closed loop and commenters traced it to an expired build. Shows silent degradation when an update is missed.

evidence_strength: Mixed and mostly indirect. Peer-reviewed observational, survey and qualitative studies (Lum 2021 n=558; Wong 2022 n=874/46; Suttiratana 2022 n=72; Huhndt 2022 n=56; O'Donnell 2023 n=129; Cleal 2025 n=383; Crabtree 2022 n=317 HCPs) record technical burden and component sourcing as leading barriers and reasons to stop. One RCT (CREATE) records hardware and connectivity withdrawals. The consensus statement and Diabetes Canada give professional guidance. The most specific and current operational detail (expiry rules, iOS breakages, pod-fault trends) comes from community documentation and newsletters, which are authoritative on mechanics but not independently verified. No peer-reviewed study measures build or maintenance hours, expiry-related events or phone-loss incidents.
prevalence_or_magnitude: Burden is near-universal for self-builders. Every iOS user must act at least every 90 days (browser build) or every week (free-account Mac build). AAPS users face enforced expiry. Loop shipped 10 releases between Jan and Nov 2026, many of them hardware or iOS fixes. Among non-users, 50% of caregivers lacked the skills to build, 42.9% feared they could not maintain a system, and 33.3% did not know where to source components (Huhndt 2022). Among users, connectivity or communication problems were 27% of reported issues and hardware failure 10% (Lum 2021). Of the 5.3% who stopped Loop, 22.2% said it was 'not working properly' and 22.2% that they 'spent too much time on it' (Wong 2022). In CREATE, 2 of 44 AID participants (4.5%) withdrew for connectivity or hardware issues. Community analytics put the per-user monthly DASH fault rate at about 4% in Nov 2025 rising to about 18.5% in Apr 2026 [uncertain: unpublished community data, denominator not given]. On the clinician side, 73.5% of UK HCPs were at most 'somewhat confident' describing setup (Crabtree 2022). Scale: BC Diabetes estimates Loop has been installed for more than 100,000 people worldwide [uncertain: unverified estimate].
data_quality_caveats: Study samples are self-selected, tech-confident, mostly white, higher-income and privately insured (Suttiratana: 95% white, 73% income of $100K or more). That is survivorship bias: the people the build burden kept out are missing. Most data is self-reported and cross-sectional, and the barrier surveys use small item denominators (n=24-28). Peer-reviewed data predate browser builds (2023), automatic certificate renewal (2025), Omnipod 5 support (2026) and current iOS versions, so they understate today's mechanics and miss new failure modes. Community fault-rate analytics are unpublished. The Wong 2022 abstract and table disagree (27.8% vs 33.3%). Cleal 2025 carries a published correction. Clinic and community documents conflict: BC Diabetes describes free-account builds lasting three months and says Omnipod 5 pods are incompatible, while LoopDocs says weekly rebuilds for a free account and supports Omnipod 5 from v3.14.7.
clinician_perspective: Clinicians generally do not see building, signing or troubleshooting the app as their job, and professional guidance backs that view. The 2022 international consensus notes that systems have 'no call-in helplines', that 'updates have to be performed manually by the user', and that clinics should document that they 'cannot take any responsibility for the system'. It expects HCPs to help with settings if experienced and otherwise refer on. Diabetes Canada (2023) calls these systems 'DIY' precisely because the user builds and maintains them, and warns that guidance goes stale fast. What clinicians fear: unsupported hardware failures out of hours, older out-of-warranty or second-hand pumps (the consensus recommends in-warranty devices), cybersecurity (the 2019 Medtronic recall covered exactly the loopable pumps), invalidating manufacturer or NHS pump warranties (28% of UK HCPs), professional reputation (31.8%), and their own lack of technical knowledge (63%). Only 8.8% of UK HCPs were extremely confident describing setup, and 59% were uncomfortable giving ongoing support (Crabtree 2022). Canadian practices see a median of only 1-5 DIY users, too few to build familiarity (Morrison 2022). What they need: a quick, reliable read of whether the system was actually closed-loop and working during a period, which app version and hardware the patient is on, a clear failure and backup plan (pen, meter, scheduled basal or MDI, sick-day rules), and a way to tell a hardware or app fault apart from a settings problem. BC Diabetes shows one alternative: the clinic takes on the build (its own TestFlight distribution), standardises the hardware (Omnipod and Dexcom, iPhone 13+), and tells users to turn off automatic iOS updates.
effect_on_relationship: The build-and-hardware layer splits care in two. Peers (Looped and BC Diabetes Facebook groups, Loop and Learn, Zulip, Discord) become the 'informal help desk', and the clinic is left with prescriptions and settings (Suttiratana 2022). Users learn not to bring technical problems to clinic. Many providers 'lacked knowledge' to troubleshoot, and one told a patient 'I am not messing with your settings' while still prescribing supplies. That narrows what gets disclosed and can push people to switch providers. Visits that should be about glycemic patterns get taken up by hardware logistics: requests for DASH pods or Omnipod training, a G7 or Libre switch, a prescription for a bridge or legacy pump. Unexplained data gaps also come up: open-loop periods after expiry, G7 dropouts or pod faults that look like non-adherence or bad settings [uncertain: inferred from failure modes; no study of misinterpretation found]. Trust can be lost either way. Clinicians may read frequent failures as proof that the system is unsafe, and users may read clinician unfamiliarity as incompetence. Among caregivers, 44.4% reported no HCP support because of limited technical expertise, and 88.9% said an HCP recommendation would motivate them (Huhndt 2022), so technical support from the clinic is a lever on the whole relationship. Where the clinic owns the build (BC Diabetes), the relationship flips: the clinic is the installer of record, writes hospital letters, and offers weekday email support next to the peer group.
decision_ownership: The user or caregiver decides almost everything: build method, when to update, whether to accept an iOS update, which branch or customisations to use, hardware sourcing (including second-hand pumps) and switching hardware. Peers and the volunteer developers (LoopKit, Loop and Learn, Trio, AAPS) set de facto rules through documentation and release gating (for example, 'don't update iOS until cleared'). Clinicians control only the regulated inputs: prescriptions for pumps, pods and CGMs, pump training sign-off, and letters for school or hospital. Liability sits with the user under the consensus disclaimer model ('clinic cannot take any responsibility'). Manufacturers disclaim off-label use (Insulet does not support Loop). Under clinic-run models like BC Diabetes, the clinic takes on build, distribution and configuration, and manages its risk through signed consent and waiver forms.
disclosure_risk: Moderate to high. Users may hide hardware details, such as second-hand or out-of-warranty Medtronic pumps, imported pods, or pump or pod use 'off-label' with Loop, for fear of losing prescriptions or support. Fear of losing HCP support was a top barrier (39.3% of caregivers; a main barrier for adults in O'Donnell 2023), and one Loop discontinuer cited fear of provider disapproval. Technical failures go to peers rather than the clinic, so the clinic rarely hears about expiry lapses or fault clusters.
regulatory_status_dependency: Yes, strongly. Cleared Loop derivatives (Tidepool Loop, cleared Jan 2023 and delivered through partner products; Sequel twiist, App Store app released Apr 2025, full US launch early 2026) remove self-building, TestFlight or certificate expiry, GitHub or Apple account upkeep and the RileyLink or legacy-pump hunt. They add manufacturer support lines, warranties and validated iOS compatibility. Phone dependency and iOS-update caution remain, and twiist currently supports only certain CGMs (reported as Libre 3 Plus and Eversense 365) [uncertain: CGM list from secondary source; Android availability not verified]. They are US-only and need a prescription.
workarounds: Browser builds instead of a Mac. Monthly scheduled automatic builds, plus automatic certificate renewal (ENABLE_NUKE_CERTS, Loop 3.6.0+) and non-expiring GitHub tokens. Calendar reminders and in-app expiry warnings (Loop warns from about 20 days out; AAPS from 28 days). Keeping a current TestFlight build ready to reinstall. Turning off automatic iOS, macOS and Xcode updates and waiting for the 'all clear' from Loop and Learn. Using the Build Select Script on a Mac. Keeping a spare phone, a spare pod, a RileyLink-type bridge, a pen and meter safety kit, and scheduled basal as the fallback. Buying used Medtronic pumps with checks (serial number, video). Switching DASH to Omnipod 5 pods or using Pod Keep Alive on iPhone 16/17e. Using community 'magnet trick' and scan options for G7. Asking peers (Looped, Loop and Learn, Zulip, Trio Discord, BC Diabetes group) for help, or having someone build remotely. Clinic-run installation (BC Diabetes SOS-AID, which distributes builds through the clinic's TestFlight). Moving to commercial AID (Omnipod 5, Control-IQ, 780G, iLet, twiist) to get rid of the burden.
existing_tools: LoopDocs, Loop and Learn (newsletter, version-update page, Build Select Script, LoopFollow, LoopCaregiver), TrioDocs and AAPS docs (builders and readthedocs). GitHub Actions with Fastlane and TestFlight. In-app expiry display and alerts in Loop, plus a 'Report a Problem' section and Issue Report export; AAPS version checker. LoopFollow 'Looping App Expire' alarm (Trio). Nightscout devicestatus (uploader battery, pump and pod status, SAGE/CAGE). Tidepool uploads. Dexcom Clarity and Glooko for CGM data only. Loop community usage analytics (opt-in), used to spot DASH fault trends. Insulet and Dexcom fault reporting channels. BC Diabetes Nightscout pre-configuration and clinic TestFlight.
existing_tool_coverage_gap: None of these tools tells the clinic, in clinical terms, how well the system was working. Missing are: the share of time actually closed-loop, open-loop periods and why they happened (expiry, comms loss, CGM gap, pod fault), app version and expiry date, iOS version, and hardware inventory and age (pump model and firmware, pod type and lot, CGM generation). Nightscout and LoopFollow show live status to the family but no period summary for a visit. Clarity and Glooko see only CGM or pump data and cannot see the algorithm layer [uncertain: Glooko Loop support not verified]. Expiry and update tracking lives with the user, and nothing escalates a lapse to a caregiver or clinic. Fault trends exist only as community analytics, not per patient. Nothing produces a standard 'technical status and backup plan' document a clinic could file, or give to a school or hospital.
data_artifacts_involved: App name, version, branch and build date; TestFlight or provisioning expiry date. iOS or Android version and phone model. Pump model and firmware, pod type (Eros, DASH Atlas, Omnipod 5) and lot, pod faults (for example 0xCB/203). CGM type and generation (G7 10- or 15-day, Libre). RileyLink or bridge status. Loop Issue Report, Nightscout devicestatus, closed- vs open-loop time, CGM gap log, temp-basal log, change history.
unmet_need: A shared, low-effort record of how healthy the system was over a period, separate from glucose outcomes, that both patient and clinic can trust. Specifically: (1) a way to tell whether poor glucose in a period came from the algorithm and settings or from the system not running (expiry lapse, open-loop time, comms loss, CGM gaps, pod faults); (2) a current, dated inventory of app version, expiry, phone and OS, pump or pod type, firmware and CGM, so prescriptions, training and switches match what the patient actually uses; (3) proactive warnings before expiry, risky OS updates or known-bad hardware combinations (for example iPhone 16/17e with DASH Atlas pods) that reach caregivers and, with consent, the clinic; (4) a standard backup and failure plan that clinicians can endorse and attach to school or hospital letters without having to understand the build. Nothing today lets a clinician support a looper's hardware and technical reality without becoming tech support, and nothing lets the user disclose that reality without risk.
implication_for_collaboration_tool: Treat system health as a first-class, clinician-readable layer. (a) Automatically capture and show a 'system status' card per visit window: app, version and build date, expiry countdown, iOS or Android version, phone model, pump or pod type and firmware, CGM generation. Flag known risky combinations from a maintained compatibility list, using LoopDocs, Loop and Learn and AAPS release notes as sources. (b) Compute and visualise closed-loop percentage and categorise open-loop or no-data periods by cause (expired app, comms loss, CGM gap, pod fault or change) so clinicians do not misread technical gaps as non-adherence or bad settings. (c) Send expiry and update reminders and 'safe to update iOS?' guidance to patients and caregivers, with an optional clinic notification for paediatric or high-risk patients. Never push code or builds; stay a read-only collaboration layer to limit regulatory exposure. (d) Produce printable or shareable documents a clinician can sign: backup plan (pen, meter, scheduled basal, sick-day rules), hardware list for prescriptions and refills, and letters for hospital admission and school phone exemptions. (e) Make disclosure low-risk: present the hardware and technical layer neutrally ('device in use') with a clear statement of the clinic's role, following the consensus documentation guidance, so users stop hiding second-hand or off-label hardware. (f) Support clinic-run models like BC Diabetes (cohort view of versions, expiry dates and hardware across a clinic) and peer handoff (link to Loop and Learn or Trio resources rather than expecting the clinic to fix builds). (g) Cover Loop, Trio, iAPS and AAPS vocabularies and failure modes. Keep working when a patient moves to twiist or another commercial system, carrying over the hardware history.
severity_rank: Medium. This is mostly carried by the user and peers, and clinicians are not expected to fix builds. But it drives what gets disclosed, how supplies and prescriptions are requested, unexplained data gaps and device switching, all of which shape trust at visits.
safety_criticality: Medium. Most failures fall back to scheduled basal (Loop within about 30 minutes) or to LGS or open loop (AAPS). The usual result is lost automation and hyperglycemia rather than acute overdose. Risk rises with unnoticed lapses overnight or in children, pump or pod faults (rising DASH 203 faults), CGM dropouts, second-hand or out-of-warranty pumps, and release bugs (for example Loop 3.6.3 fixed wrong interrupted-bolus amounts). Published cohorts report no DKA and few device-attributed severe hypos (Lum 2021: 1 attributed to Loop) [uncertain: no incidence data on expiry- or phone-loss-related DKA or severe hypoglycemia].
equity_impact: Hardest on Android-only users (Loop, Trio and iAPS need an iPhone; AAPS now needs Android 12+), people with older phones (iPhone X and 8 dropped; iOS 17.6 minimum) or Intel Macs (macOS 27 is Apple Silicon only), and people who cannot pay US$99 a year for an Apple Developer account, a newer phone or legacy pumps. Also hard on people with low digital literacy or time, older adults, and children whose care depends on a parent's technical skill. Non-English speakers rely on mostly English documentation and peer forums [uncertain: partial translations exist]. People in regions where compatible pods, pumps or CGMs are not sold are excluded, as are people with poor bandwidth (Xcode downloads). Study samples are 95% white and high-income. School phone bans add friction for children [uncertain: DIY-specific evidence not found]. Clinic-run builds (BC Diabetes) and cleared App Store versions reduce, but do not remove, these gaps.
